title: Smoke battery and hypothesis playbook for VPC/on-prem installs
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is a lightweight, hypothesis-driven smoke battery and troubleshooting playbook for VPC / on-prem Redwood runtime installs and post-upgrade sanity checks. It is intentionally compact so SREs, solutions engineers, and install engineers can run through a fixed set of probes, form a minimal set of hypotheses, and either remediate or escalate with clear artifacts.

When to use:
- Fresh install that failed beyond the bootstrap logs
- Post-upgrade anomalies (latency spikes, service crashes, missing model artifacts)
- Intermittent runtime errors observed during customer validation

High-level triage flow (5–30 minutes):
1) Gather: customer environment (VPC vs on-prem), TF module version, runtime image tag, kernel/driver versions, and exact error logs (systemd/journalctl + runtime logs).
2) Smoke battery: run the ordered probes below and capture outputs in a single paste.
3) Form hypotheses: use the failure signature matrix to map likely root causes.
4) Remediate small fixes (restart service, increase disk, reapply TF target). If >2 changes needed, open an incident and snapshot state.
5) Escalate with artifacts and suggested rollback window if needed.

Quick data to collect (minimal evidence):
- terraform state list | wc -l
- kubectl -n redwood get pods -o wide / docker ps -a
- journalctl -u redwood-runtime --no-pager -n 500
- /var/log/redwood/runtime.log (or mounted path)
- nvidia-smi (if GPU) or lspci | grep -i nvidia
- df -h and free -m

Smoke battery (ordered probes)
Note: execute in order; early probes are fast and eliminate broad classes of failures.

1) Network and DNS sanity (1–2 min)
- curl -sS -I http://localhost:8080/health || curl -sS -I https://localhost:8443/health
  Expected: 200/OK or JSON health object. Failure mode: connection refused / SSL handshake error -> runtime not listening or cert mismatch.
- dig +short storage.example.internal || host model-store.internal
  Expected: IP resolve. Failure mode: DNS failing -> VPC route or CoreDNS problem.
- ip route show and iptables -L -n
  Expected: correct default route and no unexpected block rules that drop outbound to artifact stores.

2) Control plane connectivity (2–4 min)
- curl -sS -X GET "http://localhost:8080/v1/models"
  Expected: list of loaded model metadata. Empty or 503 -> model asset problem or runtime bootstrap failure.
- grpcurl -plaintext localhost:50051 list (if grpc exposed)
  Expected: service list. Failure mode: mismatched runtime binary or port conflict.

3) Storage & artifacts (2–6 min)
- ls -la /opt/redwood/models || stat /mnt/models/metadata.json
  Expected: model folders present and manifest readable.
- head -n 20 /opt/redwood/models/<model>/manifest.json (check checksum, url)
  If model missing: check terraform outputs for object store creds and region.

4) GPU/CUDA checks (if applicable) (1–3 min)
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total,driver_version --format=csv,noheader
  Expected: GPU present & driver >= required version. Failure: driver/kernel mismatch, container runtime not exposing devices.
- docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:11.8-base nvidia-smi
  Use similar check for containerd setups.

5) Runtime process health (1–3 min)
- ps aux | grep redwood-runtime or kubectl -n redwood describe pod <pod>
- journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 200 | sed -n '1,200p'
  Look for repeated stack traces, OOM kills, or failing liveness probes.

6) Latency/cost smoke (optional quick probe)
- curl -sS -d '{"input":"hello"}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://localhost:8080/v1/generate -w '
HTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s
'
  Expected: < 500ms local CPU; < 150ms on warm GPU for short prompt. If >3s, check batching config and queue depth.

Common failure signatures and hypothesis mapping
- "Connection refused" on /health -> runtime crashed, service not started, or port conflict. Check systemd unit, container logs. Remediation: service restart; if crash loop, collect core dump and escalate.
- "Model manifest missing" -> TF outputs for object store misconfigured or model sync job failed. Hypothesis: IAM/creds or region mismatch. Remediation: check terraform outputs, re-run model sync job, validate signed URLs.
- "CUDA driver not found" / nvidia-smi missing -> host-level GPU driver not installed or incompatible. Remediation: reinstall matched driver, coordinate maintenance window; fallback to CPU variant if available.
- Repeated GC/latency spikes -> KV cache misconfiguration (cache size too small), or batching micros. Remediation: temporarily reduce max_batch_size and enable immediate flush; add ephemeral capacity if dedicated.

Terraform module upgrade notes (practical heuristics)
- Upgrade ordering: (A) provider & backend pin check, (B) infrastructure (VPC, subnets, security groups), (C) node pool / compute, (D) runtime tf modules (service resources), (E) bootstrap / model-sync scripts.
- Keep module changes small. Every upgrade should have a plan that can be applied with -target and reverted via state snapshot.
- Before rolling module upgrade: terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan; save plan and plan.json for audit.
- If a module changes resource names/IDs, run terraform state list | grep <module> to find drift.
- Typical quick rollback: terraform apply -target=<resource> -var-file=previous.tfvars OR restore terraform state from state snapshot and re-apply. Document the exact snapshot key.

Safe canary and rollback playbook (during upgrades)
- Canary pattern: upgrade one node-pool/compute-group, or one zone, and route a subset (5–10%) of traffic. Monitor: latency, 5xx rate, pod restarts, model-load errors for 15–30m.
- If canary fails: revert the node-pool changes; if the failure is a runtime config change, flip the feature flag or revert the config map and roll restart.

Automated probes & scripts (copyable snippets)
- collect-smoke-bundle.sh (example output format)
  mkdir -p /tmp/smoke-bundle && 
  cp /var/log/redwood/runtime.log /tmp/smoke-bundle/ || true && 
  journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 1000 --no-pager > /tmp/smoke-bundle/journal.txt || true && 
  kubectl -n redwood get pods -o wide > /tmp/smoke-bundle/pods.txt || true && 
  tar -czf /tmp/smoke-bundle-$(date +%s).tgz /tmp/smoke-bundle

- small TF commands to inspect state
  terraform workspace show
  terraform state list | sed -n '1,200p'
  terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars -out=upgrade-plan.tfplan

Decision thresholds (eyes on metrics)
- If 5xx rate increases >0.5% absolute during canary -> fail fast.
- If median p95 latency > 2x baseline -> pause rollout and investigate.
- If pod restarts > 1 per 5m per pod -> treat as crash-loop and rollback.

Escalation & runbook hygiene
- When escalating, attach: smoke-bundle tarball, tf plan file, exact runtime image tag, output of nvidia-smi (if GPUs), and last 500 lines of runtime log.
- Tag incident with customer, deployment-id, terraform module version, and model tag. Use Slack channel #private-deployments and the oncall SRE.
- For complex rollbacks, include a proposed time window and client-facing message draft.

Appendix: quick remediation recipes
- "Cert mismatch" on https health: check /etc/redwood/certs and the configured hostname; if cert auto-generation failed, re-run bootstrap cert task or copy certs from known good host.
- "OOMKill" on runtime: increase systemd LimitMEM or adjust container memory request/limit; check for runaway model size or infinite loop in prompt handling.
- "TF apply hangs" on creating ENI: check cloud provider quotas and rate limits; often resolved by retry after increasing quotas or breaking Terraform apply into smaller targets.

Notes and known brittle areas:
- CoreDNS in VPCs is often misconfigured for split-horizon DNS; validate that model artifact hostnames resolve inside the nodes.
- Cloud provider IAM role changes often manifest as silent 403s when fetching artifacts — check signed URL access from the node itself.
- Upgrading the runtime image without a corresponding config bump (KV cache size, token limits) frequently triggers stability regressions.

Open questions / TODOs for follow-up:
- Add a small synthetic load generator that validates p95 latency post-upgrade (controlled qps).
- Integrate smoke-bundle into our TF pipeline to automatically collect on failed apply.

Contact points:
- Private deployments eng: #private-deployments (Slack)
- Oncall SRE: sres-oncall@redwood.ai
- Escalation: eng-leads (Priya Nair)

If you run this playbook and still see an ambiguous failure, include the smoke-bundle and the terraform plan output in the incident. Keep this doc lightweight; if a pattern repeats, we will move it into the canonical private-deploy playbook with a dedicated remediation script.
